propositions.statement: Orion delivers each job to a worker for execution.
An execution is one delivery that ends in success, failure or timeout.
Executions per job are capped: one original execution may be followed by no more than three retry executions.
A job has one original execution.
The original execution is additional to the three permitted retry executions.
Once three retry executions have ended without success, the job must not be executed again.
Before every retry attempt the worker must wait exactly five seconds.
The retry wait is measured from the end of the failed attempt.
The retry delay is a single fixed pause and must not be shortened or lengthened based on attempt number.
An individual execution may run for no longer than half a minute.
When the execution time limit is reached the execution must be stopped.
An execution stopped at the time limit must be recorded as a failed attempt and the retry rules apply.
While a job is active, a further delivery is ignored only when it carries the same job id and the same idempotency key as the active job.
A further delivery with the same job id but a different idempotency key must be rejected as conflicting input and must not change the active job's state.
Deliveries may carry a producer-chosen idempotency key.
Orion must retain each idempotency key for twenty-four hours after it is first seen.
After the retention period the key may be forgotten and a later delivery with the same key is treated as new.
Delivering a job grants the worker a lease that marks the job as in hand and keeps other workers away from it.
A worker lease must last ninety seconds from the moment the job is delivered to the worker.
When the lease expires without renewal or release, the job must become available to other workers.
A worker must renew its lease when twenty seconds of lease life remain, provided work on the job is progressing.
A worker must never renew the same lease more often than once every fifteen seconds.
A renewal must extend the lease by the full lease duration from the moment of renewal.
Producers and operators can cancel jobs.
After a job is cancelled, no future execution attempt of that job may be started.
Cancellation must not interrupt an already running execution attempt; that attempt runs to its own completion, failure or timeout.
If Orion receives a cancellation for an already cancelled job, the job remains cancelled and the repeated cancellation must not otherwise change the job's state.
After the final unsuccessful execution attempt, Orion must automatically move the job to the dead-letter queue.
A job in the dead-letter queue must not be executed again unless explicitly resubmitted.
When three dead-letter events occur for the same tenant within the escalation window, Orion must raise an operator escalation.
The tenant dead-letter escalation window is one hour.
The one-hour window must be measured from the first of the three events.
Orion's execution-order promise is narrow and limited so that a slow job in one partition never stalls the others.
First-in-first-out execution order must be guaranteed only among jobs in the same queue partition.
No ordering guarantee is made between jobs in different partitions.
Each job state change produces an audit event.
Audit history must remain queryable for thirty calendar days from the moment each event is recorded.
Once an audit event is older than the retention window it may be deleted.

sentences_to_account.text: Orion delivers each job to a worker for execution.
One delivery that ends in success, failure or timeout is an execution.
Because some jobs can never succeed, the number of executions per job is capped.
One original execution of a job may be followed by no more than three retry executions.
Once three retry executions have ended without success, the job must not be executed again.
Q-31 is executed once and then retried three times without success.
Q-31 is not executed again.
Once an execution has failed, Orion pauses before delivering the job again so that a transient fault downstream has a chance to clear.
Operational review found that a growing pause made recovery times unpredictable for tenants; the delay is therefore a single fixed pause again.
Before every retry attempt the worker must wait exactly five seconds, measured from the end of the failed attempt.
The wait must not be shortened or lengthened based on the attempt number.
Q-31 fails at 08:14:10; its first retry starts no earlier than 08:14:15, and every later retry likewise starts no earlier than five seconds after the preceding failure.
Workers can stall.
To keep a stalled worker from holding a job forever, every execution is subject to a time limit, after which the execution is treated as a failure and the retry rules take over.
An individual execution may run for no longer than half a minute; when that limit is reached the execution must be stopped.
An execution stopped at the limit must be recorded as a failed attempt.
Job Q-31's retry starts at 08:15:00 and is still running at 08:15:30; Orion stops it and records a failure.
A producer that times out may send the same job again, but two deliveries that share a job id are not necessarily the same request: a producer may reuse a job id for different payloads.
Orion therefore uses the idempotency key to decide whether a repeat is genuinely the same request.
While a job with a given job id is active, a further delivery must be ignored only when it carries both the same job id and the same idempotency key as the active job.
A further delivery that carries the same job id but a different idempotency key must be rejected as conflicting input and must not change the state of the active job.
Q-52 (key IK-1) is delivered at 11:00 and is active.
A delivery of Q-52 with key IK-1 at 11:02 is ignored.
A delivery of Q-52 with key IK-2 at 11:03 is rejected as conflicting.
Deliveries may carry a producer-chosen idempotency key.
Orion keeps recent keys so repeats can be recognised.
Orion must retain each idempotency key for twenty-four hours after it is first seen.
After the retention period the key may be forgotten and a later delivery with the same key is treated as new.
Key IK-77 first appears on Thursday at 13:00; it is recognised at Thursday 23:00 and forgotten by Friday 14:00.
Delivering a job to a worker grants that worker a lease.
The lease tells Orion the job is in hand and keeps other workers away from it.
Field experience shows that sixty seconds was too short for workers that perform a cold start before their first renewal.
A worker lease must last ninety seconds from the moment the job is delivered to the worker.
When the lease expires without renewal or release, the job must become available to other workers.
Worker W-2 receives Q-40 at 09:30:00 and goes silent.
At 09:31:30 the lease lapses and Q-40 can be handed to W-5.
A worker that is still making progress renews its lease so that the job is not reassigned underneath it.
Renewal is driven by remaining lease life rather than a fixed cadence, and is rate-limited so that many workers cannot flood the lease service.
A worker must renew its lease when twenty seconds of lease life remain, provided work on the job is progressing.
A worker must never renew the same lease more often than once every fifteen seconds.
A renewal must extend the lease by the full lease duration from the moment of renewal.
W-2 holds a ninety-second lease on Q-40 from 09:30:00.
It renews at 09:31:10 (twenty seconds remaining); the lease now ends at 09:32:40, and W-2 may not renew again before 09:31:25.
Producers and operators can cancel jobs.
Cancellation tells Orion to stop investing in the job; it does not reach into a worker and abort work already under way.
Because producers retry their own requests, Orion may receive the same cancellation more than once; a repeated cancellation is simply acknowledged.
After a job is cancelled, no future execution attempt of that job may be started.
Cancellation must not interrupt an execution attempt that is already running; that attempt runs to its own completion, failure or timeout.
If Orion receives a cancellation for a job that is already cancelled, the job must remain cancelled and the repeated cancellation must not otherwise change the job's state.
Q-40 is cancelled while its second execution is running; that execution finishes on its own terms and no further execution follows.
A second cancellation for Q-40 arrives a minute later; Q-40 stays cancelled and nothing else about Q-40 changes.
A job that has spent its attempt budget without succeeding is parked for inspection rather than left blocking the queue.
After the final unsuccessful execution attempt, Orion must automatically move the job to the dead-letter queue.
A job in the dead-letter queue must not be executed again unless explicitly resubmitted.
Q-31 exhausts its attempts at 08:20; Orion places it in the dead-letter queue at 08:20 with no operator action.
Many dead-letter events for one tenant in a short time usually mean something systemic.
Orion raises an escalation when that pattern appears.
When three dead-letter events occur for the same tenant within one hour, Orion must raise an operator escalation.
The one-hour window must be measured from the first of the three events.
Tenant T-7 produces dead-letter events at 08:20, 08:45 and 09:10; the third falls within an hour of the first, so an escalation is raised.
Orion offers a narrow consistency promise about execution order.
Producers that need strict sequencing place related jobs in one partition; producers that do not need it gain throughput by spreading work across partitions.
The promise is deliberately limited so that a slow job in one partition never stalls the others.
First-in-first-out execution order must be guaranteed only among jobs in the same queue partition.
No ordering guarantee is made between jobs in different partitions.
Q-70 then Q-71 are enqueued into partition P-9; Q-70 starts first.
Q-72 in P-10 may start before, between or after them.
Each job state change produces an audit event used for investigations and tenant reports.
Audit history is kept for a bounded period so that investigations have a predictable window.
Audit history must remain queryable for one month, defined here as thirty calendar days from the moment each event is recorded.
Once an event is older than that window it may be deleted.
An audit event written on 2 June must remain queryable through 2 July and may be removed afterwards.
